clue.text: Goal foul? Suspect that might develop devastatingly

definitions.text: Goal foul? Suspect that might develop devastatingly

indicators.note: devastating means wrecking, so the three words before it are wrecked and rebuilt

explanation.surface: A football fan, seeing a foul near goal, suspects something nasty is about to unfold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'devastatingly' signals an anagram of GOAL, FOUL and SUSPECT (fifteen letters); the whole clue then reads as a description of a biblical swarm that develops and devastates crops.
explanation.definitionFit: A swarm of insects descending on fields is the classic example of a sudden, ruinous visitation.

clue.text: The leverage of money to spend

definitions.text: The leverage of money to spend

parts.words: The leverage of money to spend
parts.note: purchase can mean grip or leverage, so the phrase reads both as leverage and as what spending money can buy

explanation.surface: An economics definition of what cash in hand lets you do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Purchase' also means leverage or grip, which is why the clue speaks of the leverage of money.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the economists' term for how much goods a sum of money can buy, its buying strength.

clue.text: But this sale's knock down prices keep getting higher

definitions.text: But this sale's knock down prices keep getting higher

parts.words: But this sale's knock down prices keep getting higher
parts.note: a sale advertising knock-down prices normally means falling prices; here the hammer knocks lots down while bids rise

explanation.surface: A complaint about a sale whose bargains keep going up in price.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knock down' looks like 'cheap', but at this sale the auctioneer knocks each lot down with a hammer after the bidding has pushed the price up.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods at such a sale go to the highest bidder, the hammer falling when bids stop rising.

clue.text: Exercises customs

explanation.surface: A short note on what drills and traditions have in common.
explanation.definitionFit: To exercise a power is to employ it; and established usages or habits are customs.

clue.text: Initial Belgian course becoming hard to understand

indicators.note: becoming means turning into something else, so the letters are rearranged into a new word
the initial of a word is its first letter, so only the start of Belgian is taken

explanation.surface: A first course on Belgium that turns out to be baffling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Initial' takes B from Belgian; 'becoming' rearranges B with COURSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Something murky or cryptic is difficult to grasp.

clue.text: Put in a few words for converting coin into mere French

indicators.note: into tells us the reworked letters go inside the French word

parts.note: a mere is a lake, and lake in French is lac

indicators.note: converting means changing the form, so the letters of coin are rearranged

explanation.surface: A tidy instruction to change a coin into French money, said briefly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mere' is not 'only' but a lake, whose French word is used; 'converting' rearranges the coin's letters, and 'into' sets them inside that word.
explanation.definitionFit: Speech that is terse and spare is said in as few words as possible.

clue.text: The gang boasted

explanation.surface: The gang showed off.
explanation.definitionFit: A team of workers or a band of people is a gang; and an old past tense of crow, to brag, means boasted.

clue.text: Support us in a matter of colour

indicators.note: in places the pronoun inside the colouring word

parts.note: a stain is colouring matter, as for wood
taken as written

explanation.surface: An appeal for backing in a dispute about race or colour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a matter of colour' sounds like a political issue but is simply a dye, STAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: To uphold or keep up something is to bear it, prop it up.

clue.text: Reverse one's point of view about Heaven and Earth?

definitions.text: Reverse one's point of view about Heaven and Earth?

parts.words: Reverse one's point of view about Heaven and Earth?
parts.note: changing your view of sky and ground can be done literally, by turning the body upside down so the earth is above

explanation.surface: Someone having a religious change of heart about the cosmos.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue sounds like a change of belief, but a gymnast upside down literally has the earth above and the sky below.
explanation.definitionFit: Balancing upside down on the crown swaps sky and ground in your view; the idiom also means doing anything to oblige.

clue.text: Wobbly tickers causing wobbly legs

indicators.note: something wobbly is unsteady, so the letters of the word next to it are shaken up

explanation.surface: Unsteady hearts leading to unsteady legs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tickers' looks like hearts but just gives its letters to the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: A childhood vitamin D deficiency disease softens bones, leaving bowed, weak legs.

clue.text: China football team

explanation.surface: A national side from the People's Republic.
explanation.definitionFit: A London porcelain works made famous ware of that name; and a London club plays football in the Premier League.

clue.text: Frigid greeting?

parts.note: a cold welcome, read literally as a salutation word that also names ice falling from the sky

explanation.surface: A cold, unfriendly welcome.
explanation.walkthrough: A frosty greeting sounds unfriendly, but the word for a greeting also names frozen rain.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a salute ('All hail!') and pellets of ice that fall in storms.

clue.text: The poet who chars.

explanation.surface: A question of which poet does the cleaning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'chars' suggests a cleaning lady, but here it is the verb to scorch. Robert Burns is Scotland's national poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Scotland's best-known poet, Robert, shares his surname with the verb meaning scorches or blackens.

clue.text: for another turning dull

indicators.note: turning means the word is read the other way round

parts.note: drab means dull and dreary

explanation.surface: A follow-on to the previous clue: one more poet who has gone dull.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue leans on the clue before it: 'another' means another poet. 'turning' reverses DRAB.
explanation.definitionFit: A poet is a bard, so the second versifier the clues ask for is one too.

clue.text: Oils mixed with lacquered finish, so won't run

indicators.note: mixed means stirred together, so the letters of Oils are rearranged
the finish of a word is its last letter, so only the end of lacquered is taken

explanation.surface: A painter's tip: oils with a lacquer finish will not drip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finish' sounds like a varnish coat but takes the last letter, D, of lacquered.
explanation.definitionFit: A substance that is firm and not liquid does not flow.

clue.text: Carter's homeliest address

parts.note: the most familiar way to address a man called James Carter is by his pet name, as the US president was known

explanation.surface: Where a carter or US president lives most cosily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'address' sounds like a home location but means a form of address; President Carter's pet name was famously used officially.
explanation.definitionFit: The familiar short form of James is what friends would call him.

clue.text: NCOs order you to start PE for passing out fit

indicators.note: order as a verb means arrange, so the letters are put into a new order
to start means only the beginning of the word you is used

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Sergeants ordering recruits to start physical training until they are fit for a passing-out parade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'order' rearranges NCOS with Y (the start of 'you'); 'passing out' is a military parade in the surface but fainting in the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Medically, a sudden temporary loss of consciousness is a faint.

clue.text: A French bun from recipe of-nigh on century

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred

indicators.note: a recipe mixes ingredients, so the letters of the words after it are mixed

explanation.surface: Instructions for a French pastry from a recipe nearly a hundred years old.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bun' is a pastry in the surface but a knot of hair in the definition; 'recipe' rearranges NIGH into HIGN, and ON is kept as written.
explanation.definitionFit: The French-named coil of hair worn at the nape is a kind of bun.

clue.text: How to feed our island in nightmarish extremities?

indicators.note: in places the middle pieces between the outer letters
the extremities of a word are its first and last letters

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A wartime question of how to feed a besieged island nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremities' takes the first and last letters of nightmarish, and 'in' places the other pieces between them. The surface evokes a besieged island running short of food.
explanation.definitionFit: To give food and sustenance is to sustain or nurture.

clue.text: All the same, nurse might put it on

explanation.surface: A remark that a nurse might get dressed anyway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'All the same' looks like 'nevertheless' but is the adjective meaning identical throughout.
explanation.definitionFit: Constant and unvarying means all the same; and the regulation outfit is what a nurse wears on duty.

clue.text: Monotonous droning over a cylinder

indicators.note: in a down clue, over means the first piece sits above the second

parts.note: a droning sound is a hum
a drum is a cylinder

explanation.surface: A dull droning over a cylindrical engine.
explanation.definitionFit: Something dull, routine and repetitive is tedious.

clue.text: A master of time-keepers among the atom pioneers

indicators.note: among means the letters lie inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: A pioneer of timekeeping among the early atomic scientists.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Tompion was a celebrated 17th-century English clockmaker. 'among' signals the letters inside 'atom pioneers'.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous English clock and watchmaker is called the father of English watchmaking.

clue.text: Trade in the streets

explanation.surface: Commerce conducted out on the roads.
explanation.definitionFit: To deal or barter, often illicitly, is to trade; and the vehicles moving along the roads are what fills the streets.

clue.text: Help turning up in first North American state

indicators.note: first tells us the word in goes at the front

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up means the word is read from the bottom up

parts.note: aid means help

explanation.surface: Aid arriving in the first North American state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning up' reverses AID to DIA; 'first' puts IN at the front, and NA finishes it.
explanation.definitionFit: This Midwestern US territory is one of the fifty in the Union.

clue.text: Caught by highwayman, I forked out

indicators.note: caught by means held inside, so the letter goes inside the word for the robber

parts.note: a pad, as in footpad, is an old word for a highway robber

explanation.surface: A traveller held up by a highwayman paid up.
explanation.walkthrough: PAD (short for footpad) is an old word for a robber on the road; 'Caught by' puts I inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To fork out money is to hand it over, settle the bill.

clue.text: A sticky patch with bucking mares

indicators.note: a bucking horse throws itself about, so the letters of the word mares are thrown about

explanation.surface: A rider having a sticky time with horses that keep bucking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sticky patch' sounds like a bad spell but is a literal smudge.
explanation.definitionFit: A smudge or blot of something greasy is a dirty mark.

clue.text: Scraps of chances

explanation.surface: A small piece of betting talk.
explanation.definitionFit: Odd bits and leftovers are scraps; and a bookmaker's prices express probabilities, or chances.

clue.text: In which Hebrews measured grain heap, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters may be some other arrangement of the word next to it

explanation.surface: Ancient Hebrews measuring a pile of grain.
explanation.walkthrough: The ephah (also spelt epha) was an ancient Hebrew dry measure, about a bushel.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient dry measure used by the Israelites for grain held roughly a bushel.

clue.text: Ruin United Nations party

parts.note: a do is a party or celebration

explanation.surface: A party at the United Nations ends in ruin.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring someone to destruction or downfall is to wreck them.

clue.text: Maybe thrasher who quietly gets through

parts.note: taken as written
p is the musical marking for piano, quietly
per means through or by means of

explanation.surface: A bird-watching note: perhaps it is a thrasher that slips through unnoticed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'thrasher' looks like the bird but is one who thrashes; to whop is to thrash, so a thrasher is one who whops.
explanation.definitionFit: To whop is to beat, so one who beats or thrashes is one who whops.

clue.text: Loud trumpeting about first supporter joining soccer bosses

indicators.note: joining means the next pieces are attached in sequence

parts.note: a fan is a supporter
the FA, the Football Association, governs English soccer
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: A loud celebration as a leading fan meets the football authorities.
explanation.walkthrough: The FA (Football Association) runs English football; 'first' puts the supporter at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: A flourish of trumpets, as for a royal arrival, is a burst of brass.

clue.text: Labourer from Scotland who intervened twixt Bald win and Baldwin

definitions.text: Labourer from Scotland who intervened twixt Bald win and Baldwin

parts.words: Labourer from Scotland who intervened twixt Bald win and Baldwin
parts.note: a Scottish Labour Party leader who became prime minister between two spells of the Conservative Stanley Baldwin, the first a slim victory

explanation.surface: A Scottish worker who came between a hairless winner and a man named Baldwin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labourer' means a Labour Party man, not a manual worker. Ramsay MacDonald, a Scot, was Britain's first Labour prime minister, in 1924, between Stanley Baldwin's governments.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scottish Labour leader held office as prime minister between Conservative Stanley Baldwin's terms.
